Il y a deux ans, en plein mois d’août, M: Two years ago, in the middle of August, Mentor Avdiu, then 42, was busy repairing the oven of a restaurant on Bernard Street in Montréal’s Mile End. During his breaks, he watched the neighbourhood. Across the street stands the iconic storefront, decked out with birdcages, of Tammy, a florist originally from Hong Kong who ran several businesses in the area back when rents were affordable and her children were young.
La boutique de Drawn and Quarterly, le m: The shop of Drawn and Quarterly, the legendary publisher of alternative comics, is barely a minute away. Farther along there is Dépanneur Café, with its whimsical morning concerts, and the Brazilian restaurant, once a must-visit, which recently closed its doors.
Comme les quelques autres rues qui relie: Like the few other streets that link the Mile End to the affluent borough of Outremont, this stretch of barely two kilometres has two sections, each with its own character. On the Outremont side, the avenue is wider, lined with residential buildings, high-end boutiques and restaurants opening onto spacious sidewalks.
De ce côté, la rue Bernard mène à la voi: On the other side, Bernard Street leads to the railway line that served the local factories for much of the 20th century. For several generations, the nearby residential buildings housed the immigrant working class, before it headed off to the suburbs. There were the Irish Catholics, the traditional Jews who came from the Russian empire in the early 20th century and, farther along, where the two Bernard Streets meet, the Hasidim, the southern Italians and the Greeks who arrived after the Second World War.
« Cette partie de la ville illustre parf: “This part of the city perfectly illustrates its diversity,” says Justin Bur, a neighbourhood historian. Starting in the 1980s, families of young professionals and high-tech companies slowly replaced the aging immigrant communities and the abandoned factories.
Il y a 10 ans, cet embourgeoisement est: Ten years ago, this gentrification became so visible that it caught the attention of Gen X Germans and the New York Times, which further contributed to rising real estate prices.
Cependant, ce n’est pas ce que M. Avdiu: That is not what Mr. Avdiu noticed, however, as he walked the street in the summer of 2020. What he mostly saw was the culmination of a lifetime of effort, for he had left his native Albania on foot as a teenager, headed for Greece, before starting a thriving appliance repair business in Montréal. He had made it. He wanted to celebrate having made it and, above all, to convince his son to come back and live with him.
C’est ainsi que les choses se sont passé: That is how it happened, according to Mr. Avdiu. “You know, I could open a café here,” he told the manager of the restaurant whose oven he had just fixed. The manager pulled him toward the door next door. “Go talk to those guys,” he suggested.
Deux anciens petits commerces, un cordon: Two former small businesses, a shoemaker and a barber, were then adjoining the restaurant. They belonged to the same Greek family that had settled in the neighbourhood in the 1960s and was now thinking of moving to the suburbs. Mr. Avdiu, who speaks Greek, quickly struck a deal.
Pendant les mois qui suivent, il entrepr: Over the following months, he set about transforming the space with his family’s help. He knocked down the wall separating the two shops and replaced the front doors with glass. He covered the walls with brick and dressed them with lacquered wooden shelves. Wooden beams run across the white-painted ceiling. On one side, he put in a counter, where he placed an espresso machine, and set up a board listing the menu. On the shelves, he has set out packages of the house coffee blend, coffee makers and black-and-white photos of the Old Continent. Bistro tables and chairs furnish the space, which also has a couch draped with a shawl in the colours of the Albanian flag.
Durant les Fêtes, on peut y voir un <em>: During the holidays, you can see a qeleshe, the traditional Albanian headwear, and a box of pandoro, an Italian Christmas cake. On the other side of the room are a small empty counter and a large rectangular table. The owners will figure out later what to do with them. And they did all of this with their own hands. The place is so pretty that a friend of Mr. Avdiu’s, an interior designer, makes no secret of her astonishment. He named the café “Lori,” after a well-known coffee brand in Albania, which is also the name of his own roasting company. The café opened its doors in December 2020, in the middle of the pandemic, and his son Dimitri left Greece to come and manage it.

C’est en janvier 2013 que Mentor Avdiu d: It was in January 2013 that Mentor Avdiu landed at Pierre Elliott Trudeau Airport intending to claim political asylum. “What am I doing here?” he wondered when he saw the winter. Within a month, he landed a job repairing appliances at a shop owned by Greeks. He cycled there until he figured out how to get around by bus. His brother and his son joined him at the end of the year and, in 2015, he regularized his status. It was not the first time he had undertaken such a journey.
L’Albanie, un pays des Balkans situé au: Albania, a Balkan country in southeastern Europe, has three million inhabitants.
Il est bordé par la Grèce et l’ancienne: It is bordered by Greece and the former Yugoslavia, and lies across the Adriatic Sea from Italy. Since the collapse of communism in 1989, hundreds of thousands of people, perhaps more than a million, have fled a declining economy and taken refuge in Greece and Italy, where they work in precarious jobs. Even today, Albanians make up a significant share of the immigrant communities in those countries.
Mentor se souvient qu’à l’automne 1995,: Mentor remembers that in the fall of 1995, barely 13 years old, he travelled with his father to a small town in central Greece, six days away on foot. There he harvested olives.
Plus tard, il a de nouveau pris le chemi: Later, he once again took the road to Greece on foot, this time never to return. He became an apprentice in an appliance repair shop. He was so gifted that two years later, he was travelling all over Greece and even going as far as Italy to repair espresso machines. After a brief stint at the Greek subsidiary of Danesi, the Italian coffee machine manufacturer, Mr. Avdiu went into business for himself. More than anything, he wanted to honour the advice his father had given him since childhood. He was determined to have a decent job and to own his own business.
« Tu dois aller en Amérique du Nord », l: “You have to go to North America,” his father often urged him. It was the land of opportunity. “To the United States, if you can. But Canada is good too,” he told him. Mr. Avdiu tried every means to reach America, but it is particularly difficult for Albanians to obtain a visa. He had no Greek documentation that would have allowed him to enter Canada without having to give a reason. He ended up getting a fake Greek passport on the black market and trying his luck at the airport. That is how he entered the country.
En l’espace de cinq ans, M. Avdiu met su: Within five years, Mr. Avdiu had set up his repair business in Saint-Laurent, then expanded his activities to transporting roasted coffee beans between distributors and businesses.
À son entrepôt de Saint-Laurent, les aff: At his Saint-Laurent warehouse, business was going well, and the company employed a dozen people. His brother also had his own construction company. His son Dimitri, however, could not stand the winters. And above all, he had left love behind. In 2016, at 21, he took the road back to Greece and became a bouncer in nightclubs in Patras, a port city where he would make his home for nearly 10 years. Though he was troubled to see his son so far from him, Mr. Avdiu kept building a life in Quebec.
En raison de la proximité de l’Italie, l: Because of the proximity of Italy, the Albanian population gradually became avid espresso drinkers, the joke being that Albania produces the best espresso outside Italy. By specializing in espresso machine repair, expertise that took him to Italy, Mr. Avdiu became a true espresso enthusiast.
Et il n’a pas réussi à se satisfaire des: And he could not bring himself to be satisfied with the products available here. So, with the help of a friend, he began roasting his own blend of coffee beans. He started preparing a blend that was both bitter and dense, close to the one he was used to in Europe. A few cafés in the city adopted it. But who could have said that one day, Mentor Avdiu would have a café of his own?
Dimitri s’est marié en Grèce, et son tra: Dimitri had married in Greece, and his work as a nightclub bouncer eventually wore on him. “You have to bring him back here,” advised a friend who had just visited his own son in Patras.
M.Avdiu m’a raconté avoir eu une longue: Mr. Avdiu told me he had a long phone conversation with his son when he signed the lease on Bernard Street. “I said to him: ‘Are you ready to run the business? You can’t let me down.’ [Dimitri] hesitated a little, but he finally made up his mind and said yes.” That is how he came back to Montréal. The two men started out serving muffins and bureks, those savoury pastries wrapped in phyllo dough that Greeks call pitas, and the bitter espresso favoured by members of the Albanian community. The latter are not necessarily regulars of the neighbourhood.
La population, estimée à quelques millie: The population, estimated at a few thousand people, is mostly scattered across the suburbs and the neighbourhoods with a larger presence of newcomers, namely Saint-Laurent, LaSalle, Côte-des-Neiges and, farther out, Laval, Longueuil and even Terrebonne.
Sont d’abord arrivés les étudiants franc: The first to arrive were francophone students, or those who had studied in France and already knew the language. The Greek crisis of 2010 brought hundreds more, many of whom went looking for work in the Greek businesses on Parc Avenue. Then came the construction workers.
<strong>‍</strong>En mars dernier, Dimit: ‍Last March, Dimitri kicked an Albanian customer out of the café. His father and he had unfurled the Romani flag on the counter, in the unoccupied part of the space. The customer complained: “You’re ruining everything with that,” he said. Dimitri, who can have a short fuse, told him: “You get out of here right now or I’ll throw you out. I don’t need your dirty money.”

Les Avdiu sont des Roms d’Albanie. Le pa: The Avdius are Roma from Albania. The country is home to tens of thousands of Roma, a number sometimes estimated at nearly 100,000. Mentor Avdiu belongs to the Mechkars, a Romani people who, in central Albania, specialize in agricultural work.
Si de nombreux Roms ont émigré, les Roms: While many Roma have emigrated, Albanian Roma are few in number in Montréal. In Levan, the village where Mr. Avdiu grew up in Albania, 24 people were killed in 1997 during a conflict between Roma and non-Roma Albanian gangs. And even though he was not there – he was living in Greece at the time – he no longer wanted to endure this racism. In 2015, he even obtained his political asylum claim documents by citing the endemic racism he had faced all his life. Nevertheless, he knows how to navigate among Roma and non-Roma, and many of his friends are Albanian. The television in the corner of the room plays Albanian music on low volume and, through the speakers, another Albanian music channel can also be heard.
Soixante-dix pour cent de la clientèle d: Seventy per cent of Café Lori’s clientele is Albanian, including people who come in on Sundays from the suburbs, construction workers who stop by for their coffee break and a French interpreter who advises asylum seekers through their administrative procedures. The coffee tastes “like the one we have at home,” they say. Greeks also frequent the place, notably Dimitri’s friends who have just settled in Montréal.
L’entrepreneur entame sa journée de trav: The entrepreneur begins his workday by calling his mother in Albania, his daughter, who stayed in Greece, and his partner, also in Albania.
Il espère pouvoir les faire venir ici un: He hopes to bring them here one day. Then he heads to Saint-Laurent, to his appliance repair shop. After that he stops by here, on Bernard Street, at Café Lori. He does not expect his industry to bounce back anytime soon. It is hard to find permanent staff. The pastry maker who used to make bureks had to stop working because of family problems, and at Lori they now serve spanakopitas and tiropitas prepared by a Greek supplier.
Le café vient d’obtenir un permis qui lu: The café has just obtained a permit that will allow it to set up a sidewalk terrace over the summer. Things will work out in the end. What matters most to him is that his family stays close. Last year, Mr. Avdiu became the grandfather of a little boy named Hysni, whom he looks after on weekends while the family gathers on the café’s couch. Mentor Avdiu explains that the Romani flag has been displayed in his café since last February out of pride. Being Roma is an identity that has shaped his life, that of a hard worker with good business sense from a very close-knit family who, whatever the path, will make it through.
Ce qu’il souhaite, c’est organiser une f: What he wants is to organize a Roma celebration so that the whole community can come to Café Lori. And they are beginning to flow in – slowly but surely. Nik, a 23-year-old chemical engineering student, is a Rom from Greece. He is sitting at a table in the café. Outside, the comings and goings of young professionals, students, immigrant elders who still live in the neighbourhood and Hasidim set the rhythm of neighbourhood life. “You may call this place an Albanian café,” says Nik, sipping an espresso.
« On y entend parler albanais, c’est vra: “You hear Albanian spoken here, it’s true. But for me, it will always be the Roma café, the place where I can speak my language, where people understand me and answer me in that language.”
